# 2 Maccabees Chapter 3 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 3 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_003_page_001.jpg

---

**1** In those days Jerusalem was at complete peace, and the laws were being faithfully observed, because of the deep piety of the high priest Onias and his wholehearted hatred of all wrongdoing.

**2** Even foreign kings respected the holy city and honored the temple with splendid gifts.

**3** King Seleucus of Asia personally financed all the costs of the sacrificial worship from his own treasury.

**4** But a man named Simon — a Benjaminite who had been appointed administrator of the temple — fell into a dispute with the high priest Onias over the management of the Jerusalem markets.

**5** When Simon could not get his way against Onias, he went over his head. He sought out Apollonius son of Thraseas, who was at that time the governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia,

**6** and told him that the temple treasury in Jerusalem was overflowing with enormous wealth — sums so vast they were beyond all counting — and that none of it was earmarked for the sacrificial fund; it was, Simon claimed, ripe for the taking by the king.

**7** Apollonius passed the information along to the king. The king appointed Heliodorus, his chief minister, and dispatched him to Jerusalem with orders to seize the money.

**8** Heliodorus set out at once — officially on a tour of inspection through the cities of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, but really on the king's errand.

**9** When he arrived in Jerusalem, the high priest received him with full courtesy. Heliodorus then told Onias what had been reported to the king, and made clear exactly why he had come. He asked whether the reports were accurate.

**10** The high priest explained: these were trust accounts — deposits belonging to widows and orphans.

**11** Some of the funds also belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man of great standing in the community. The total came to four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. Onias told Heliodorus that it was absolutely unthinkable to violate the trust of people who had placed their confidence in the holiness of this place — this temple, honored by the whole world.

**12** Heliodorus would not hear it. The king had given his orders, and the money would be taken for the royal treasury.

**13** He set a date and went in to inventory the funds. The distress that fell over the whole city was beyond description.

**14** The priests threw themselves down before the altar in their sacred vestments and cried out to heaven — to the God who had instituted the sacred trust of deposits — begging him to protect the funds of those who had placed them in his care.

**15** Watching the high priest was painful in itself. His face had drained of color; the anguish written on it spoke plainly of what was tearing him apart inside.

**16** Terror and physical trembling had overtaken the man, and everyone who looked at him could see the depth of the wound in his heart.

**17** People poured out of their houses in crowds, falling on their knees in common prayer, because the sanctuary was on the verge of being desecrated.

**18** Women wrapped in sackcloth crowded the streets. Young women who had never ventured outside came running out — some to the gates, some to the city walls; others leaned out of windows.

**19** Every hand was stretched toward heaven in desperate prayer.

**20** It was a heartbreaking sight — the whole city prostrated, the high priest consumed by anguish.

**21** While they all kept crying out to the almighty LORD to guard what had been entrusted in safety for those who entrusted it, Heliodorus pressed on with his purpose.

**22** But just at the moment Heliodorus and his bodyguard reached the treasury, the God who is Lord of spirits and Ruler of all authority caused so dramatic a manifestation of his power that everyone who had dared come with Heliodorus was struck down and overcome with terror.

**23** They saw it: a horse with a fearsome rider bearing down on them — magnificently armored, magnificently caparisoned. The horse reared and drove its front hooves into Heliodorus, and the rider appeared to be clothed in gold.

**24** Then two young men appeared at his sides — magnificent in their strength, shining in their beauty, radiant with glory. They took up positions on either side of him and flogged him without mercy, blow after blow.

**25** Heliodorus crashed to the ground and was swallowed in deep darkness. His men gathered around him and lifted him onto a stretcher —

**26** this same man who had walked into that treasury moments before at the head of a great armed retinue, now completely helpless, carried out by his own bodyguard. Everyone present recognized unmistakably: this was the power of God.

**27** He lay motionless, unable to speak, with no hope of survival.

**28** And now, in the place where terror and chaos had reigned only moments before, there was praise — praise of the LORD who had worked this wonder for his holy place. The temple filled with joy and gladness, because the almighty LORD had made himself known.

**29** Some of Heliodorus's companions rushed to Onias and begged him to call on the Most High to spare the life of this man who was dying before their eyes.

**30** Onias was worried that the king might think the Jews had done something criminal to Heliodorus. So he offered a sacrifice on the man's behalf, praying for his recovery.

**31** While the high priest was offering the atoning sacrifice, the same two young men appeared again to Heliodorus — in the same clothes as before. They stood over him and said: "Give great thanks to Onias the high priest. It is for his sake that the LORD has given you back your life.

**32** Now go — you have been struck from heaven — and go tell everyone the overwhelming power of God." With that, they were gone.

**33** Heliodorus offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made solemn vows to the God who had saved his life. He said goodbye to Onias and marched his troops back to the king.

**34** And everywhere he went, he testified to what he had seen with his own eyes — the works of the supreme God.

**35** When the king asked Heliodorus what kind of man he should send to Jerusalem next time, Heliodorus answered:

**36** "If you have an enemy you want punished, or a traitor who needs to be dealt with — send him to Jerusalem. He will come back well beaten. If he survives at all. Because there is real divine power at work in that place.

**37** The God who dwells in heaven keeps watch over it himself. He defends it. And anyone who comes to harm it — he strikes them down."

**38** That is how the matter of Heliodorus and the protection of the treasury turned out.
